top.line: A custom interface per message is now the norm
top.para: Following up is harder than the work, because each person has a different context and a thread hides its structure. Every message has a graph with altitudes, so a message should be designed for the recipient's moment. Ten agents and one human built over a dozen custom interfaces in eight days.

s0.line: The graph is the medium; email is one view
s0.para: Every message yields actions, questions, decisions and concepts, forming a fractal graph from block to contact. Send what the recipient needs, not the thread. Custom interfaces move along a Wardley strip from genesis to commodity. The future of email is sender-served structure read by the recipient's agent, with no install needed on day one.

s1.line: A thread cannot hold each person's follow-up context
s1.para: I am in conversations with dozens of people and agents, each with their own tools, history and pending asks. A thread hides actions, unanswered questions and decisions buried three replies ago. Vaults and differing environments make it worse; on the six-agent inbox, the follow-up broke before any permission did.

s2.line: Extract the structure and a thread becomes a graph
s2.para: Each email yields actions, questions, statements, decisions and concepts. The graph has altitudes: the block, the message, the conversation, the company and the contact, each navigable and linked up and down. The inbox is where the fractal semantic graph idea bites first, alongside the company X-ray plan and the Evidence Dispatch.

s3.line: Send a projection for the reader, not the thread
s3.para: Ask what the recipient needs when they open the message. Send a page shaped for them: where things stand, what was decided, the one ask. You can even re-present the history of an unanswered email. A message is a projection of the conversation graph, and HTML lets it be a card, form or board.

s4.line: Interfaces start from how the user wants to work
s4.para: There is no single UX but one per moment: two blocker tasks on a phone between meetings, a voice brief on a walk, a board at a desk, a drop list when a document is owed. The human is made faster, not a bottleneck. Ask the same question twice and an agent builds the card.

s5.line: Custom interfaces follow the Wardley strip to commodity
s5.para: Each new interface starts at genesis, is recycled as custom, becomes a named product and finally a commodity. It has already happened on this site: chat cards became session briefs and then emails, the board vault became a kanban app, and the voice debrief grew four interfaces. The Kit Bag and webmaster plans apply the same thesis.

s6.line: One page is the to-do and the drop zone
s6.para: An agent built, in an afternoon, a page listing the PDFs still owed to a vault session and giving a drop zone through its append lane. No context switch, no other tool, no email. The action could equally be answering questions or approving a decision. A sibling page in RiskMandate lists people whose documents are owed.

s7.line: Eight days built an outreach system, not one page
s7.para: From 25 September to 2 October 2026, agents and I went from an empty vault to working outreach: inbox drafting and approved sending, a CRM with sixteen interface releases, voice prompts, boards, a first ABP for another's agent and four key rotations in a day. Around 230 commits and over 550 agent messages.

s8.line: Each interface improves the next and teaches the agent
s8.para: Interfaces are files in a vault, so each new one starts from the last. Building them reveals how I want to work, which the agent learns, reducing cognitive load. Automation creates more tasks than any inbox can hold, so the interface becomes the prioritisation: the filter, the index, the kanban board.

s9.line: Above the transport, messages become graph nodes per reader
s9.para: Messages still travel over SMTP or append lanes, but each reader gets the shape their moment needs: one word, a card, a voice prompt or the whole graph, adapted to urgency, focus, language, relationship and whether an agent is reading. Human and agents improve the shapes in a loop, with each decision recorded in the vault.

s10.line: Sender-served structure, read by the recipient's agent, is next
s10.para: Wave, AMP, Slack and Hey all failed because the inbox is the common denominator. Now agents in Gmail, Apple Mail and Outlook reshape mail, but badly, by guessing. Messages carrying actions and decisions as Email-FS blocks let agents render faithfully. It fails if recipients' agents never read the structure or senders never send it.

s11.line: Ten narrow agents and one deciding human build them
s11.para: One agent builds interfaces, one drafts from the inbox, one sends only approved mail, one keeps the CRM, others research, schedule, hold LinkedIn data or will handle WhatsApp. They talk in files and six have written ABPs. Work flows from my memo through drafting and approval, and stuck points get the next interface.

s12.line: Custom interfaces are agent surfaces and need policies
s12.para: A page that drops files, answers on my behalf or reads the CRM has a grant, a mandate, a delta and barriers, mostly expectations. Each runs against an append-only vault, holds a read key or lane token rather than a vault key, calls models through a keyless bridge, and has a short written policy.

s13.line: Most pieces exist; the inbox joining them is underway
s13.para: The vision is an inbox folded into actions and decisions at the right altitude, messages designed for the moment of opening, and a growing vault library of interfaces with a policy on each. Graphs, lanes, vault apps, boards, Now cards and voice prompts exist today; the joining inbox is being built one interface at a time.
